## Scoring Frame — What This Pass Is Actually Testing

This pass scores the **six propositions carried out of the distinctiveness check**, not the earlier candidate set. Those six are the live field: the present-tense ambition line, the name-as-threshold line, the standing line, the composure line, the temperament line, and the instinct line.

One calibration decision governs every Brand Permission judgement below. The combined house is assessed as it now exists — **a merged Jaguar with an electric, petrol and hybrid range** — which means the 2021 all-electric commitment is a superseded plan and no proposition is penalised for sitting outside it. What does remain live as permission evidence is anything that bears on how this house behaves toward customers after the sale: the documented dependability record of the group and the **September 2025 cyber incident** that halted production and disrupted retailer and customer systems. Those facts are applied only where a proposition makes an ownership or standing claim, and they are applied hard there.

> The sharpest finding in this set is that the strongest lines draw their defensibility from the brand's own name rather than from a service promise the house cannot yet evidence.

---

## The Field Assessment

Two propositions carry genuine structural locks. **The name-as-threshold line** converts the badge into a behavioural standard, and because no rival in premium automotive is named after a creature whose behaviour can be invoked, the sentence is close to unsayable by anyone else. **The composure line** attacks the one axis the category has left unguarded — not more capability, but the complete concealment of it — and it is underwritten by a competition record that is historical fact.

The weakest links are the ownership-facing claims. Where a proposition asks to be judged on how customers are received and kept, the house has no published standard and a recent, highly visible operational failure. That is not a reason to eliminate those lines, but it is the reason their permission scores sit low and must be surfaced for human judgement rather than buried.

> A claim about standing is only as strong as the most recent week in which the house was asked to deliver it.

SELECTION RULE: Truth Strength ≥ 5 AND Competitive Impossibility ≥ 6 are hard floors. Below either eliminates. Fame, Brand Permission, Clean Air and Commercial Precedent surface human flags but do not eliminate. Weighted composite out of 90 (the six weights total 90) is computed in code.

SMP: "One house. Every ambition. Including the one you have now." — FIELD: Present-Tense Ambition
Fame: 7/10 — The third clause is a genuine turn and lands as a statement about the reader's life rather than the manufacturer's lineup, but at ten words across three beats it is a line people will notice and agree with rather than repeat verbatim, and the brand does not sit inside the sentence to travel with it.
Truth Strength: 7/10 — Grounded in a verifiable range architecture organised by life stage rather than rank — three SUVs on sale now spanning a documented price ladder from roughly US$51,200 beneath a US$130,500 electric GT — which is a category truth this house can credibly access; it falls short of the top band because the "every ambition" breadth depends on 2027–2030 product that is client-supplied and unverified.
Competitive Impossibility: 6/10 — Difficult but not impossible with repositioning. Mercedes-Benz has already run this move at model level with "Grow Up" (2018) for the A-Class, legitimising the entry buyer's present want, and could extend that argument to the house without contradicting "The Best or Nothing"; the deduction is named against that specific campaign and position rather than against general availability.
Brand Permission: 8/10 — Strong standing from documented product fact: a single badge carrying a three-row family SUV, a style SUV, a presence SUV and an electric GT with no junior marque beneath it, which is the structural precondition for the claim. Deduction cited to the verified YouGov consideration and buzz movement following the November 2024 rebrand, which is named evidence that existing belief in the badge is currently unsettled rather than stable enough to extend effortlessly.
Clean Air: 8/10 — Territory available with only weak and distant competitive presence. The nearest named activity is Mercedes-Benz "Grow Up" (2018), a single-model entry campaign that has long since ended and never claimed the house-wide present-tense position; no competitor currently occupies this territory as a brand platform.
Commercial Precedent: 7/10 — Close structural precedent carried by two named post-2000 campaigns: IKEA "The Wonderful Everyday" (2014), which built an entire platform on dignifying the life being lived now rather than the life being saved for, and Mercedes-Benz "Grow Up" (2018), which commercially succeeded by addressing present-stage want in a premium automotive context. Both post-2000 precedents carry the score; no pre-1980 example is relied upon.
CODE VERDICT: PASS — clears Stage 10 hard floors (Truth Strength ≥ 5, Competitive Impossibility ≥ 6).
CODE COMPOSITE: 63.5/90 weighted (Fame 30% · Truth 20% · Competitive Impossibility 15% · Brand Permission 10% · Clean Air 10% · Commercial Precedent 5%).
CODE FLAGS: none

SMP: "The jaguar doesn't share its name lightly." — FIELD: The Name As Threshold
Fame: 8/10 — People will notice and remember the brand because the brand is the subject of the sentence; the line is quotable, slightly severe, and carries its own mythology without requiring a supporting idea to explain it.
Truth Strength: 7/10 — Grounded in a genuine owned asset, the literal behaviour and meaning of the brand's own name, combined with the real single-badge architecture that leaves nowhere to hide a weaker car. It sits below the top band because the threshold it implies — cars that qualify or are refused — is not yet documented brand behaviour with a published record.
Competitive Impossibility: 9/10 — Possible only through fundamental contradiction. The closest named analogue is BMW's "The Most Powerful Letter in the World" (2016), which treats a conferred badge as a withheld honour, but that is a sub-brand letter inside a numeric hierarchy; the creature-name lock here is semantic ownership a rival cannot replicate, since Mercedes class letters, Audi rings and Lexus's invented word describe position rather than behaviour and have no temperament anything could fail to meet.
Brand Permission: 7/10 — Credible standing from the name itself and from the founder-era "Copy Nothing" dictum the house has publicly revived. Deduction cited to a specific named product fact: the current volume entry model's documented specification — a 268 hp four-cylinder with no hybrid at 22/27 mpg — which is checkable in a showroom this weekend and sits in measurable tension with a claim that the name is granted only to cars that earn it.
Clean Air: 8/10 — Territory available with weak and distant competitive presence. BMW's M-badge honour framing is adjacent but operates on a sub-brand letter, not on the house name as a behavioural standard; no competitor occupies the specific territory of the marque name functioning as a threshold a car must pass.
Commercial Precedent: 8/10 — Close precedent. BMW M "The Most Powerful Letter in the World" (2016) is a named post-2000 campaign built on a badge conferred rather than distributed, and Mercedes-AMG "One Man, One Engine" (platform active through the 2010s) is a named post-2000 expression of a mark earned through a standard. The 2016 BMW campaign carries the score; Patek Philippe's 1996 generations line is noted as illustrative only and does not contribute.
CODE VERDICT: PASS — clears Stage 10 hard floors (Truth Strength ≥ 5, Competitive Impossibility ≥ 6).
CODE COMPOSITE: 70.5/90 weighted (Fame 30% · Truth 20% · Competitive Impossibility 15% · Brand Permission 10% · Clean Air 10% · Commercial Precedent 5%).
CODE FLAGS: none

SMP: "Change the car. Keep the standing." — FIELD: Standing Held By The Person
Fame: 6/10 — Six words, two beats, clean enough to survive a boardroom and a billboard, but the sentence is abstract and brand-free, so people may register the promise without the badge travelling with it.
Truth Strength: 6/10 — Grounded in a category truth the house can credibly access, with partial specific support from the register of more than 50,000 declared interests, roughly four in five from people who had never owned the brand — affiliation recorded before any car existed. It does not reach higher because standing conferred on persons has no operational mechanism behind it in the supplied evidence.
Competitive Impossibility: 6/10 — Difficult but not impossible with repositioning. Nio's NIO House membership proposition is a named, live competitor claim that standing attaches to a member rather than to a transaction; it currently keys privileges to the vehicle and the app, but closing that gap is a programme redesign rather than a contradiction of its position, which makes the territory reachable for it.
Brand Permission: 5/10 — Partial standing with documented tension. The affiliation register is real evidence that people joined before buying. Against it stand two named facts directly relevant to a standing claim: the absence of any defined, differentiated range-wide ownership or service standard in the supplied evidence, and the September 2025 cyber incident that halted production and disrupted retailer and customer systems — the most recent public test of whether this house keeps people when circumstances change.
Clean Air: 7/10 — Adjacent competitive presence but the specific claim is available. Nio's NIO House membership platform occupies the neighbouring territory of belonging held by the person; it has not claimed the specific proposition that standing survives a move down the range, which remains open.
Commercial Precedent: 7/10 — Close precedent carried by American Express "My Life. My Card." (2004), a named post-2000 campaign that relocated status from the product to the person and succeeded commercially in a comparable media environment. American Express "Membership Has Its Privileges" (1987) is cited at partial weight only and does not carry the score.
CODE VERDICT: PASS — clears Stage 10 hard floors (Truth Strength ≥ 5, Competitive Impossibility ≥ 6).

CODE FLAGS: none

SMP: "You'll never see it try." — FIELD: Composure As The Product
Fame: 8/10 — Five words containing their own reversal, built to be said aloud and repeated, and conspicuously quiet in the loudest aisle of the category. It sits below the top band only because the brand name is not inside the line and must be supplied by the work around it.
Truth Strength: 6/10 — Grounded in a category truth the brand can credibly access, supported by a real competition record — seven Le Mans victories and the Formula E Teams' Championship — and by the long, low proportion of the design language. The deduction reflects a stretch the audience may test: the entry volume model's documented 268 hp four-cylinder specification makes effortless reserve harder to assert at the cheapest door.
Competitive Impossibility: 7/10 — Difficult but not impossible with repositioning. Lexus is the named exception: "Experience Amazing" (2016) and its founding serenity argument put it within reach of composure as a claim, though it would have to reverse "The Relentless Pursuit of Perfection", which is visible effort codified. Porsche, BMW M, Mercedes-AMG and Tesla all sell the trying as the product and would contradict themselves outright.
Brand Permission: 8/10 — Strong standing from documented history and product truth: a competition record that is historical fact, and a heritage line — "Grace, Space, Pace" — that already encodes effort held in reserve. Deduction cited to the named product specification of the current volume entry model (268 hp, 22/27 mpg, no hybrid), which is the one place the claim is immediately checkable and currently weakest.
Clean Air: 8/10 — No competitor occupies this territory. Lexus's serenity is the absence of event rather than force withheld, and no named rival currently runs a positioning claim or campaign on concealed capability; the specific territory of effort proven elsewhere and never performed here is available.
Commercial Precedent: 7/10 — Close precedent. Apple "Shot on iPhone" (2015) is a named post-2000 campaign built entirely on withholding the claim and letting the output stand, and Stella Artois "Reassuringly Expensive" (running into 2007) is a named post-2000 premium precedent for restraint as the desire mechanism. The Ogilvy Rolls-Royce line of 1958 is illustrative of the principle only and does not contribute to the score.
CODE VERDICT: PASS — clears Stage 10 hard floors (Truth Strength ≥ 5, Competitive Impossibility ≥ 6).
CODE COMPOSITE: 66/90 weighted (Fame 30% · Truth 20% · Competitive Impossibility 15% · Brand Permission 10% · Clean Air 10% · Commercial Precedent 5%).
CODE FLAGS: none

SMP: "Nothing timid about the car. Nothing careless about the ownership." — FIELD: One Temperament, Not Two Departments
Fame: 6/10 — The paired negatives have rhythm and read as human speech, but at ten words the line argues a position rather than detonating one; people will notice the sentiment and may not carry the brand away with it.
Truth Strength: 5/10 — Partially grounded. The first clause is supported by genuine, documented behaviour: the November 2024 rebrand and the Type 01's 1,015 hp specification provoked global argument, which is nerve on the record. The second clause requires a stretch the audience may not accept, because no defined, differentiated range-wide ownership or service standard exists in the supplied evidence to make "nothing careless" verifiable.
Competitive Impossibility: 6/10 — Difficult but not impossible with repositioning. Genesis is the named route: its "Athletic Elegance" design language and its valet servicing proposition give it both halves with moderate work, and nothing in its position would have to be contradicted to say this. Lexus owns the care half outright but would have to disown the carefulness-for-nerve trade it made at launch in 1989.
Brand Permission: 4/10 — Partial standing with direct, named tension on the second clause. The nerve half is well evidenced by the 2024 rebrand and the Type 01 specification. Against the care half stand three named facts: the absence of any defined range-wide ownership standard in the supplied evidence, the group's documented dependability ranking weakness, and the September 2025 cyber incident that halted production and disrupted retailer and customer systems. A line inviting audit on carelessness is at its most exposed in the year that audit was publicly failed. Flagged for human judgement.
Clean Air: 6/10 — Adjacent competitive presence but the combined claim is available. Lexus occupies the care half through "The Relentless Pursuit of Perfection" and its Takumi craftsmanship platform; no named competitor holds both clauses simultaneously, which keeps the specific dual claim open.
Commercial Precedent: 6/10 — Distant-to-close. Hyundai Assurance (2009) is a named post-2000 precedent for an ownership promise doing the selling work alongside the product and it succeeded commercially during the US downturn, but it is a single-clause move; no named campaign has successfully held audacity and care in one sentence. The Lexus Covenant (1989) carries partial weight only.
CODE VERDICT: PASS — clears Stage 10 hard floors (Truth Strength ≥ 5, Competitive Impossibility ≥ 6).
CODE COMPOSITE: 50/90 weighted (Fame 30% · Truth 20% · Competitive Impossibility 15% · Brand Permission 10% · Clean Air 10% · Commercial Precedent 5%).
CODE FLAGS:
  ⚠ BRAND PERMISSION: significant gap between this claim and demonstrated brand behaviour

SMP: "Same instinct. New territory." — FIELD: Instinct Over Habitat
Fame: 5/10 — People may notice the execution but are unlikely to remember the brand. Four words of corporate symmetry that read as an expansion announcement; without a supporting device the line does not identify whose instinct is being described. Flagged.
Truth Strength: 6/10 — Grounded in a category truth the house can access, and supported by the genuine fact of a widened range entering unfamiliar segments under one badge with electric, petrol and hybrid alongside each other. It does not score higher because "instinct" is asserted rather than evidenced by any documented product or brand behaviour.
Competitive Impossibility: 5/10 — Available to competitors with moderate effort. Lotus made precisely this argument at the Eletre launch in 2022, positioning a large SUV as the same driver's instinct carried onto new ground under the "For the Drivers" platform, and Porsche has run the same logic since the Cayenne entered the market. The word "instinct" is generic register rather than a name-derived lock, so the brand's own semantic ownership does not protect it here.
Brand Permission: 8/10 — Strong standing from documented product fact: the combined range genuinely enters new segments and new powertrains concurrently, so the claim describes what the house is actually doing. Deduction cited to the verified YouGov consideration and buzz movement after the November 2024 rebrand, named evidence that the instinct the line asks audiences to recognise is itself currently contested.
Clean Air: 5/10 — A named competitor has already moved toward this territory. Lotus "For the Drivers" (2022), launched with the Eletre, is an explicit claim that the brand's character travels intact into an unfamiliar segment, and Porsche has argued the same continuity since the Cayenne. Flagged.
Commercial Precedent: 7/10 — Close precedent carried by two named examples. The Porsche Cayenne launch (2002) is the definitive post-2000 case of a marque's character carried into alien territory with extraordinary commercial success, and Lotus Eletre (2022) repeated the structure in a comparable media environment. Both post-2000 precedents carry the score.
CODE VERDICT: ELIMINATED — Competitive Impossibility 5/10 below hard floor of 6.
CODE COMPOSITE: 51/90 weighted (Fame 30% · Truth 20% · Competitive Impossibility 15% · Brand Permission 10% · Clean Air 10% · Commercial Precedent 5%).
CODE FLAGS:
  ⚠ FAME: this proposition may not cut through in market

## What The Scores Imply For Selection

Five propositions clear both hard floors. **The instinct line falls below the competitive impossibility floor** because its central word is generic register rather than an owned asset, and because Lotus and Porsche have both demonstrably run the move — the proposition asks the brand to claim something it cannot hold.

Two human flags require resolution before the next stage. The temperament line carries a permission flag that is not stylistic but factual: a sentence inviting audit on carelessness arrives in the same year as a production-halting operational failure, and it cannot be run without the published standard it presumes. The instinct line carries both a fame and a clean-air flag and should not be revived without a device that makes the instinct visible and brand-specific.

> The strongest assets in this field are the two that borrow their defence from the brand's own name and its own competition record — the only two things in this house a rival cannot acquire, rebuild, or outspend.

Two calibration decisions govern every verdict below. First, no proposition in this set carried an Iconic Tier flag out of the scoring pass, so T8 returns N/A throughout and no downgrade is available. Second, the ownership-facing propositions are tested hard against the September 2025 cyber incident and the group's dependability record, because those are the only public evidence a sceptical reader has about how this house behaves after the sale — and two of the six lines ask to be judged on exactly that.

## Per-Proposition Pressure Blocks

### SMP: "The jaguar doesn't share its name lightly." — FIELD: The Name As Threshold — ICONIC TIER FLAG: NO

T1 — Factual Falsity: HOLDS — Rationale: The line makes no falsifiable factual assertion; it states a standard of conduct around a name the house unambiguously owns, and the semantic behaviour of the animal is not a claim anyone can disprove. The entry model's 268 hp specification creates argument, not contradiction.
T2 — Logical Incoherence: HOLDS — Rationale: A single-badge architecture in which every car carries the name is not logically inconsistent with a threshold applied before a car exists — the sentence describes what is refused, not what is rare.
T3 — Permission Failure: HOLDS — Rationale: Credible basis exists in the name itself, in the publicly revived founder-era refusal dictum, and in a single-badge range with nowhere to conceal a weak product. The absence of a published refusal record weakens the claim but does not remove its basis.
T4 — Forbidden Zone: WOBBLES — Rationale: Under interpretation pressure the threshold argument can slide toward engineering originality and uninterrupted lineage — two territories explicitly closed to a house assembled from multiple engineering origins and recently, visibly reinvented. Guard-rail required: the threshold is argued on behaviour and character, never on platform exclusivity or unbroken heritage.
T5 — Competitive Counter-Vulnerability: WOBBLES — Counter: "Some badges are given. Ours is still earned." — Classification: COMPETES-FOR-TERRITORY — Rationale: The strongest available counter comes from a performance sub-brand running an honour-conferred argument; it fights for the same emotional space rather than revealing that this house's claim is untrue, and no rival can replicate a creature-name whose temperament a product can fail.
T6 — Time Decay: HOLDS — Rationale: The defence is semantic ownership of a proper noun, which does not decay with category drift, powertrain shift or specification inflation. Naming conventions among rivals describe position, not behaviour, and that asymmetry is structural.
T7 — Interpretation Drift: CRACKS — Misreading: "Jaguar is for the few — if you are at the cheapest door, you have not earned the name." — Guard-rail: Every execution must show the entry vehicle passing the threshold, and the threshold must be stated as applying to cars, never to customers. Rationale: For a normal reader, withholding language reads as gatekeeping of people before it reads as discipline over product, which would re-erect precisely the aspirational hierarchy this house's available territory depends on dismantling.
T8 — Iconic Sustainability: N/A — Rationale: Not flagged as Iconic Tier in the scoring pass.

## Pressure Test Report

### Section 1 — Fatal failures

Two propositions fall. The temperament line fails T1 outright: its second clause makes a present-tense absolute claim about ownership care that public evidence from the September 2025 production-halting incident and the group's dependability record contradicts today, and its T5 counter was classified **EXPOSES-UNTRUTH**, which routes back to the same fatal finding rather than registering as competitive risk. The instinct line remains eliminated on the Stage 10 competitive-impossibility floor and independently fails T5 against two named rivals with two decades of prior proof.

> The only proposition eliminated on its own pressure performance is the one that asked to be audited on a behaviour the house publicly failed to deliver within the last twelve months.

### Section 2 — Competitive exposure

One surviving proposition carries a competitive flag. The standing line attracts a credible counter from a rival already operating concierge and service-collection infrastructure in live Western markets, and from a membership-house competitor holding the adjacent belonging territory. That counter was classified **COMPETES-FOR-TERRITORY** because the affiliation register — more than 50,000 declared interests, roughly four in five from non-owners — is genuine evidence that standing attaches to the person here before any car is bought. The exposure is a race, not a lie. The name-as-threshold and present-tense-ambition lines drew only wobbles at T5, from rivals who would have to extend or contradict existing positions to run the counter, and wobbles do not flag.

### Section 3 — Longevity

Three of the four survivors hold cleanly at three years. The name line is the strongest longevity asset in the set because its defence is semantic ownership of a proper noun, which no category drift erodes. The composure line wobbles against electrification making effortless delivery a default, but survives because it claims concealment of proven effort rather than mere quietness, and because rival positions are built on performing the strain. No surviving proposition carries a decay flag, because in no case could a specific dating event be named within the horizon.

### Section 4 — Interpretation risk

One flag, and it is the most consequential finding in this pass. The name-as-threshold line's most natural reading for a normal consumer is exclusion of **people**, not discipline over **product** — which would rebuild the aspirational hierarchy the house's available territory exists to dismantle. The guard-rail is specific and testable: the entry vehicle must be shown clearing the threshold in the work itself. Every other misreading identified across the set was available but not default, and was recorded as a wobble.

> A line that can be misread is normal; a line whose misreading reverses the strategy is a deployment condition, not a creative note.

No proposition entered this stage carrying an Iconic Tier flag, so T8 returned N/A across the set and no confirmations or downgrades were available. Six propositions were received and six were tested; no block was omitted and no proposition was eliminated for boldness. **SECTION 3 — STRATEGIC LANDSCAPE SUMMARY**

These four propositions are not four versions of one idea; they are three genuinely different bets about where this brand's authority comes from. **Bet one — the house belongs to the customer:** "One house. Every ambition. Including the one you have now." and "Change the car. Keep the standing." both relocate meaning from the product to the person, and both are consistent with the separately recommended One House, Every Ambition territory. **Bet two — the name sets the standard:** "The jaguar doesn't share its name lightly." makes the brand's own name the bar every car must clear, and draws its defence from an asset no rival can acquire. **Bet three — the character is the proof:** "You'll never see it try." stakes everything on composure and withheld capability, refusing the specification argument the category is built on. Two of these propositions are clear and two are exposed, and the trade-off is real: "One house" and "You'll never see it try" are the harder ones to contest or misread, while "The jaguar doesn't share its name lightly" and "Change the car. Keep the standing" claim more ground — the first claims the most defensible asset in the house but must be executed with care so it reads as discipline rather than exclusion; the second claims a territory the category has left vacant but cannot be said out loud until the business can stand behind it.

Each of these propositions leads to genuinely different work, different audiences, different cultural conversations, and different competitive positions. Selecting between them is not choosing a favourite line — it is deciding who this brand is in its market and what it stands for over the next three to five years.

## Brand Fit Validation — Jaguar: "The jaguar doesn't share its name lightly."

## Section 1 — Brand Fit Verdict

**CONFIRMED WITH ADJUSTMENTS — PROCEED.**

The proposition is tonally and culturally native to Jaguar, and it is the only available line that confronts the merger question head-on rather than decorating around it. It is not, however, currently true at the level of the whole range: three of the four vehicles that will wear the badge have not yet been re-engineered, facelifted or held against any published standard, because no such standard exists. That gap is real, but it is a gap of build sequence and governance, not a contradiction of Jaguar's model — JLR owns the assets, controls the engineering, and has already committed to the re-engineering work. The proposition therefore proceeds as a **forcing claim**: it states the bar before the bar is fully built, and its strategic value lies precisely in obliging the organisation to build it. The adjustments below govern how the claim is sequenced and earned, not how far it is softened.

---

## Section 2 — Credibility Dimension Scores

**Product Truth Alignment — 5.** Type 01 carries the claim comfortably at 1,015 hp, three motors and roughly 400 miles of range, designed and built in the UK, but the QX80, QX60 and QX65 are rebadges whose Jaguar design and character are a stated intention rather than a delivered fact.

**Audience Permission — 6.** Consideration moved from 4.3 to 6.1 in the UK and 50,000-plus registrations of interest arrived with roughly 80% new to the marque, which is permission to speak with authority — but buzz fell among adults overall, most existing owners were never expected to follow the move upmarket, and former Infiniti SUV families in the US and Gulf have no relationship with Jaguar at all.

**Tonal Compatibility — 8.** Restrained, assured, premium and design-led is exactly where this line sits; it is the tonal sibling of "Stealth by Design" and it speaks in the brand's established register of saying less with more weight.

**Behavioural Capacity — 4.** There is no published range-wide ownership standard to point at, the merger is newly underway, FY2026 finances are under pressure, and the September 2025 cyber-attack has already demonstrated that production and dealer operations can be interrupted — the brand is being asked to behave a standard it has not yet written.

**Cultural Authority — 8.** Seven Le Mans wins and the 2025/26 Formula E Teams' title give the name genuine competitive weight, and a single creature-name badge across an entire range with no junior marque beneath it is a structural authority no competitor holds.

**Historical Consistency — 5.** "Copy Nothing" and exuberant modernism sit naturally alongside a proposition about selectivity, but the brand has recently reversed a twice-stated electric-only commitment and absorbed another marque's range wholesale, which means audiences have fresh evidence that Jaguar's declarations can move.

> The most vulnerable credibility dimension is **Behavioural Capacity**: the proposition names a bar, and Jaguar currently has no published, testable definition of what that bar is or who enforces it.

---

## Section 2B — Forcing Proposition Test

Behavioural Capacity (4), Product Truth Alignment (5) and Historical Consistency (5) all sit at or below the threshold, so the test is mandatory and is run here.

**Verdict: FORCING PROPOSITION.**

The gap between claim and current reality is one of sequence, investment and governance — every component of which Jaguar controls. The path is specific and nameable: author and publish a range-wide ownership standard with testable criteria covering design, dynamic character, powertrain, service and data resilience; apply that standard as a formal pre-launch gate; complete the already-committed re-engineering and facelift programme model by model; and release each vehicle into the Jaguar badge only once it has cleared the gate, with the clearing itself becoming the launch narrative. Nothing in Jaguar's ownership structure, product economics or category role contradicts the claim — the company owns the vehicles, the engineering capability, the racing programmes that supply technical credibility, and the authority to set the bar. What it lacks is the published standard and the elapsed build time, both of which are buildable on a known schedule.

> This is the Avis condition precisely: the claim arrives first and the organisation is obliged to earn it. The strategic risk is not that the claim is untrue today — it is that the organisation fails to treat the claim as a binding commitment and lets a vehicle through the gate unchanged.

---

## Section 3 — Strategic Ownership Test

### Can the brand own this territory?

Yes, and more defensibly than any direct competitor. The territory is **the name as a threshold** — and Jaguar is the only premium manufacturer whose badge is a creature, carried across an entire range, with no junior marque sitting beneath it to dilute what the badge signifies. Competitors run tiered architectures in which an entry model and a flagship wear the same letters at very different standards; that structure makes a threshold claim literally unavailable to them. Jaguar's seven Le Mans wins and current Formula E Teams' title supply the historical and contemporary evidence that the name has meant something measurable, not merely something stylish. The defence is structural rather than communicative: as long as there is one badge and one standard, the territory cannot be copied without a competitor dismantling its own brand architecture.

### Can the brand behave this proposition?

This is where the work sits, and the requirements are concrete. Jaguar must be able to state what the bar is in terms a buyer or a journalist can check; it must be able to show, model by model, what was changed to clear it; it must apply the standard to the Type 01 as visibly as to the rebadged vehicles, so the bar reads as range-wide rather than as a remedial test applied to the newcomers; and it must be willing to delay a launch that has not cleared the gate. Behaviour also extends past the product into ownership — a proposition about selectivity is undermined by reliability perception and by a cyber-attack that interrupted dealers, because both are experienced by customers as the brand failing its own standard after purchase. The behavioural requirement is therefore a single standard covering build, character and ownership, published and enforced by a named internal gate.

### Can the brand sustain this proposition?

Over five years, sustainability depends on whether the standard survives commercial pressure. The claim compounds beautifully if it holds: each launch becomes a repeatable story of a car clearing the bar, the hybrid arrivals from 2028 extend the standard into a third powertrain type, and the single-badge architecture means every addition reinforces rather than fragments the proposition. The failure mode is equally clear — under FY2026 financial pressure, a volume vehicle is pushed through the gate without the promised re-engineering, the gap becomes visible, and the claim inverts into evidence of hollowness. Sustainability is therefore a governance question, not a creative one. If the gate has real authority to delay, the proposition strengthens annually; if it does not, the proposition has a shelf life of one compromised launch.

---

## Section 4 — Positioning Adjustments

**Publish the bar before claiming the bar.** The proposition presumes a standard that does not yet exist; the organisational input states plainly that a range-wide ownership standard will need building. Jaguar must author and publish a named, testable standard — covering design character, dynamic behaviour, powertrain, and ownership and service commitments — so that the claim refers to something external and checkable rather than to internal taste. Downstream creative, launch and retail stages must reference this standard as the proof asset; no campaign should launch that cannot point to it.

**Sequence the claim to the build programme, not to the merger announcement.** With the QX80, QX60 and QX65 pending re-engineering and facelift, a simultaneous range-wide assertion would be checkable and false. The claim should enter market at full strength on the vehicle that demonstrably clears the bar, and be extended model by model as each one does. Downstream launch planning must treat badge transfer as an earned event with its own narrative moment, never as a simultaneous relabelling exercise.

**Fix the grammatical subject as the car.** The human strategic review is binding: the name is earned by the cars and never withheld from people. Every downstream expression must make the vehicle the one being judged — the brand assesses its own products, never its buyers. Any line in which the implied object of selectivity is a person is out of brief by definition, and this applies to retail, dealer and social expression as strictly as to film.

**Hold the bar to ownership, not only to engineering.** Audience intelligence records reliability perception issues and the September 2025 attack that disrupted production and dealers. A threshold proposition that covers only horsepower and design invites the obvious rebuttal that the hard part of ownership was excluded from the test. Downstream customer-experience, warranty and dealer stages must be treated as in-scope for the standard, not as separate service communications.

**Keep the register at assurance, never adjudication.** Tonal intelligence specifies confident, restrained and premium, never snide, with the earlier "Stealth by Design" work as the reference. A threshold claim delivered with any trace of verdict-giving reads as superiority. Downstream tone-of-voice work must codify the difference between stating a standard and pronouncing judgement, and must observe the supplied constraints: no positioning against electric, no reference to the previous marque by name, build location or engineering origin, no first or only claims, and no "most powerful ever" superlative.

---

## Section 5 — Operational Requirements to Earn the Claim

- **Author and publish a named range-wide ownership standard with testable criteria** spanning design character, dynamic behaviour, powertrain, software, service and data resilience. Repairs **Behavioural Capacity**. Horizon: within two quarters, and necessarily before the first rebadged vehicle reaches market.
- **Complete the committed re-engineering and facelift on each former-Infiniti platform so it visibly carries Jaguar design and character before the badge is applied.** Repairs **Product Truth Alignment**. Horizon: model by model, each gated ahead of its own launch date rather than against a single range deadline.
- **Establish a formal pre-launch gate with named ownership and genuine authority to delay a vehicle that has not cleared the standard.** Repairs **Behavioural Capacity**. Horizon: immediate, at board governance level, and documented before any launch commitment is made public.
- **Transfer a specific, nameable set of Formula E powertrain and software learnings into the series range and document the transfer.** Repairs **Cultural Authority**, converting a racing record into present-tense product evidence. Horizon: 2026 through 2028, aligned to the hybrid introduction.
- **Upgrade the warranty and ownership promise across the entire range to a single level, with no tiering between the Type 01 and the SUVs.** Repairs **Audience Permission**, directly addressing reliability perception. Horizon: 12 to 18 months.
- **Publish a dealer and customer-data continuity standard with stated recovery commitments following the 2025 production and dealer disruption.** Repairs **Audience Permission** and **Historical Consistency**. Horizon: within 12 months.
- **Apply the same published standard to the Type 01 and show it being applied,** so the bar reads as range-wide rather than as remedial testing of the incoming vehicles. Repairs **Product Truth Alignment** and **Historical Consistency**. Horizon: at Type 01 deliveries in the second half of 2027.
- **Hold the 2028 hybrid introduction to the identical published standard, with the same gate and the same public documentation.** Repairs **Historical Consistency**, demonstrating that the standard governs powertrain choices rather than bending to them. Horizon: 2028.
- **Operate one specification floor and one service standard across all four nameplates, with no junior tier introduced beneath them.** Repairs **Behavioural Capacity** and protects the structural advantage of a single badge. Horizon: 18 to 24 months, as a standing architectural commitment.

---

## Section 6 — Strategic Commitments

**Build and publish the standard, then submit to it.** Jaguar must put into the public domain a named ownership standard with criteria specific enough that a motoring journalist can test a vehicle against them — and must then accept being measured against it. This is derived directly from the mechanism: a threshold proposition is empty without a defined threshold.

**Gate every badge transfer, including the right to delay.** No vehicle wears the name until it has cleared the gate, and the organisation must demonstrate at least once that it will move a launch date rather than lower the bar. Without a visible instance of the gate working, the standard will be read as a marketing document.

**Make each launch the documented account of a car clearing the bar.** Every model introduction must show what was changed, measured against which criterion — the engineering work made visible rather than summarised. This converts the rebadge from something to explain into the central proof of the proposition.

**Extend the standard into ownership within eighteen months.** A single warranty level, a single service standard and published operational resilience commitments across the whole range, so that the threshold governs the years after purchase and not only the moment of sale.

**Maintain a single badge with no tier beneath it.** The structural source of the brand's authority here is that no junior marque dilutes what the name means. This must be treated as a standing commitment with board-level protection against the commercial temptation to introduce an entry tier under financial pressure.
